niche.title: The Train That Rolled Through the Sea | Victorian Britain’s Weirdest Railway
niche.description:
In 1896, an extraordinary electric railway began carrying passengers through the shallow sea near Brighton, England.
Known as the Daddy Long Legs, Magnus Volk’s bizarre invention travelled on towering iron legs, with wheels rolling along tracks beneath the water.
A violent storm damaged the machine shortly after it opened—but Volk rebuilt it. The unusual railway continued operating until 1901.
It sounds impossible, but this was real Victorian engineering.
Discover the incredible story of the train that didn’t walk on water… it rolled through the sea.

niche.title: The Weirdest Victorian Weather Gadget You've Never Heard Of | #shorts #history
niche.description:
This storm alarm used 12 leeches in a circle to predict weather changes. It remains a strange example of 19th-century meteorology.

The device was designed based on a doctor's theory that leeches climb when storms approach. The mechanism functioned like a leech-sized mousetrap connected to a chain, which triggered hammers to strike a bell whenever the leeches moved upward. This antique weather instrument highlights the creative, albeit unusual, methods used to measure atmospheric pressure before modern sensors were developed.

niche.title: London's Weirdest Streetlamp Has a DISGUSTING Secret!?😱
niche.description:
London has a Victorian streetlamp designed to burn SEWER GAS! But the truth behind how it worked is even stranger.

Hidden on Carting Lane, near London’s famous Savoy Hotel, is an unusual invention called the Webb Sewer Gas Destructor Lamp.

Invented to help deal with unpleasant sewer fumes, it used an ordinary gas flame to draw gases from the sewers and burn combustible fumes.

One of London’s strangest forgotten inventions!
